Your classifier has an AUC of 0.90. You report it and everybody nods.

Then it goes live on data where 1% of the cases are positive. Seven out of eight alerts it raises are false.

Nothing broke. The AUC was right. It just answers a different question from the one you'll be asked.

## A classifier you can write on a napkin

Take the simplest scores you can think of. Negatives get a score from a normal distribution with mean 0. Positives get one with mean 1.8. Same spread for both, standard deviation 1.

The two bells overlap, but the positives sit clearly to the right. If you draw the ROC curve and measure the area under it, you get 0.90. That's a decent model, the kind you'd be happy to ship.

Now pick a threshold. Say 1.8, right on top of the positive mean. Everything above it gets flagged.

Half of the positives score above their own mean, so you catch 50% of them. That's the **true positive rate**, or recall: 0.50.

For the negatives you need the tail of a standard normal beyond 1.8. It's 0.036. That's the **false positive rate**: 3.6% of the negatives get flagged by mistake.

Recall of 50% and a false positive rate of 3.6%. On the ROC curve, that point sits far to the left and well above the diagonal. It looks great.

## Count what you flag

The ROC curve works with two rates. Each one is computed inside a single class. Recall divides by the number of positives. The false positive rate divides by the number of negatives. Neither of them knows how many of each there are.

But you don't look at rates. You look at alerts. And an alert is a mix of both classes, in whatever proportion the world gave you.

Put numbers on it. Say you score 1,000 positives and 100,000 negatives. That's about 1% positives.

You catch 50% of the 1,000 positives: **500 true alerts.**

You wrongly flag 3.6% of the 100,000 negatives: **about 3,600 false alerts.**

Of everything the model flags, the fraction that is actually positive is the **precision**:

$$\text{precision} = \frac{\text{TPR} \cdot P}{\text{TPR} \cdot P + \text{FPR} \cdot N}$$

Here, $P$ and $N$ are the number of positives and negatives. Plug them in:

$$\frac{500}{500 + 3{,}593} \approx 0.12$$

One alert in eight is real. The other seven go to someone who has to look at them and find nothing.

## Same model, other base rate

Keep the model. Keep the threshold. Change only the mix: 50% positives, 50% negatives.

Recall is still 0.50. The false positive rate is still 0.036. The ROC curve is the same curve, point for point, and so is the AUC.

But now the formula gives

$$\frac{0.50}{0.50 + 0.036} \approx 0.93.$$

Precision of 0.93, against 0.12. Same classifier. The only thing that moved was how rare the positives are.

**The ROC curve describes the model. Precision describes the model in the place where you use it.** You can't read one off the other without the base rate.

## Moving the threshold doesn't rescue you

You can ask for fewer false alarms. A stricter threshold does cut them. Here is what happens with 1% positives:

| Threshold | Recall | False positive rate | Precision |
|----------:|-------:|--------------------:|----------:|
| 1.0       | 0.79   | 0.1587              | 0.05      |
| 1.8       | 0.50   | 0.0359              | 0.12      |
| 3.0       | 0.12   | 0.0013              | 0.46      |

To get close to one real alert in two, you give up almost nine out of ten positives. Maybe that is the right trade for your problem. Maybe not. But you only see the trade if you look at precision and recall together. The ROC plot never shows you precision.

Saito and Rehmsmeier make the same point
([PLoS ONE, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0118432)). With imbalanced data, a ROC curve can look better than the model behaves. A precision-recall curve shows you the number your users actually feel.

## What this changes for you

Before you trust an AUC, ask how rare the positive class is. If it is 1%, the AUC is telling you very little about the alerts you will actually send.

I'd do the napkin calculation before reading the AUC at all. Take one operating point from your curve, multiply the rates by the real counts, and write down how many false alerts per true one. It takes four lines.

If the answer is eight, or eighty, you want to know now. Whoever reads those alerts will find out anyway.
